windows.label: Human
windows.text:
Even if I found my twin flame, she’d still be one person. The polarity could be perfect and we’d still need other people around us.
Here’s how this looks for me: whenever something serious comes up in my relationships, we each run to our own friends for support. Then I resent the one-sided story she’s telling, she resents the one-sided story I’m telling. Some of the friends may even be exes who want us to break up, and eventually neither of us wants to talk to the other’s friends anymore. That’s a pretty terrible time to be trying to run the rest of life with two people. If one person goes down, the other becomes the whole backup system for housing, money, children, health, and emotional crises. Who even has time for the relationship itself at that point?
Maybe an unusually strong couple can get away without much outside support.

windows.label: Human
windows.text: I think that’s rare.

windows.label: Human
windows.text:
But often, a friend who actually knows us both sees the dysfunctional pattern before either of us does. On the other hand, If both people are falling apart, there is only so much anyone else can do.
Separate confidants can be helpful and harmful. Sometimes you need privacy from your partner and somewhere else to say what you’re feeling. But if your confidant doesn’t have a good connection with your partner, the conversation can turn into an echo chamber very easily.
Having the same confidant creates the opposite problem: now you may not have a release valve when you want privacy from your partner, so neither way is perfect.
If you do have separate confidants, you need enough emotional maturity to remember they will automatically be biased toward you. They’re only hearing your side, usually while you’re upset, and they may just be trying to protect you, so take what they say with a grain of salt.
I lived all the permutations of this with Bee, except that we never lived in community. I suspect if we had, we might still be together. She would not have been capable of demonizing me when everyone already knew both of us and knew I wasn’t a narcissistic abuser. It would have contained all the insanity. Baseless accusations only work with friends who only know one side.

windows.label: Human
windows.text: Going slowly can show you how somebody’s moods move over time, how they treat you, and how they treat other people, but it still can’t tell you how good the sex will be or how either of you will act afterward.

windows.label: Human
windows.text: You can know somebody for twenty years and then discover on the first night that the polarity isn’t there.

windows.label: AI-Generated
windows.text: Maybe their smell turns you off, or one of you wants it every day while the other is happy with once a month. Your kinks might not line up either, or one person is sexually shut down, or your bodies just don’t click.

windows.label: Human
windows.text:
Some of those things might get better if both partners are committed to helping each other through it, but sometimes bad sexual fit still feels like, “Let’s just be friends!”
Saying, “The sex isn’t working for me,” may sound like, “I only love you if the sex is good.” But universal love doesn’t make someone special.

windows.label: Human
windows.text: It isn’t romance.

windows.label: Human
windows.text:
It’s the basis of any good relationship of any kind.
I can still love her and not want to be in a romantic relationship with her. Romantic love generally needs good sex too, or we’re friends who care deeply about each other.

windows.label: Human
windows.text: Once I’m attached, “I’m taking a chance on her” starts turning into “she’s the right person” after we’ve been together for a while.

windows.label: Human
windows.text: Based on what?

windows.label: Human
windows.text:
Sometimes I actually learned something about her, but other times all that changed is I’m attached now, and that just makes me less likely to question it.
If I have sex with somebody quickly, that’s a reason not to move in quickly too, and to keep seeing friends, have some kind of community around the relationship, and pick actual dates to ask how it’s going. Moving in together right away is basically getting into a common-law marriage without discussing it, and it’s too easy for me to assume the relationship is going well just because we’re already entangled.
I can know I want her much faster than I can know whether I want to raise children with her, live in community with her, or build a life with her.
At some point one of you will ask, “Why am I special to you? Why are you with me and not somebody else?” If the answer is basically, “We had sex and got hitched?” I don’t know, that’s a damn shame.

windows.label: Human
windows.text:
When I’m in love, I see everything just from the love angle. I should probably admit that before I give anybody more advice.
A friend in my TherapyCircle chat was talking about PTSD recently, and I said, “I have anti-PTSD.” I coined it as a joke, but even though it feels nice to have Anti-PTSD, it can leave me at more risk than if I had PTSD. Instead of expecting danger, I keep expecting each new woman and each new situation to finally be the beautiful exception.

windows.label: Human
windows.text: I see the good. I give the benefit of the doubt long after it has stopped being a benefit.

windows.label: Human
windows.text:
Then the false positive resolves into the same old pattern and gives me actual PTSD, like Ping Pong.
I grew up assuming the best of everybody because that’s what my parents taught me. Now I’m trying to be more suspicious and check for red flags before I’m alone with somebody I badly want to please.

windows.label: Human
windows.text: Why does she contact me only sometimes? What’s the pattern?

windows.label: Human
windows.text: Is she communicating enough for me to really know her interest level and what’s underneath it? Would my twin flame behave like this?

windows.label: Human
windows.text: That’s my question.

windows.label: Human
windows.text:
Not everybody is searching for somebody who will naturally channel the divine in their presence.
My second marriage to Bee is the clearest example. I knew within a week of her visiting that she saw me as her father. I didn’t know where that might lead, and it seemed like the only avenue to her heart, so I went with it.
A lot of women have seen me that way, and honestly that part can be fine. The question is whether they can hold it lightly, playfully, and curiously, or whether it turns into something all-enveloping, and they start taking everything they feel about their dad out on me as if I’m him. With Bee, the main issues were the BPD and that her aunts had badly witchcrafted her as a child.

windows.label: Human
windows.text: She would tell you the same.

windows.label: Human
windows.text:
She loved me openly and intensely and seemed to understand me spiritually. Most of all, there was the forest-and-mansion line I mentioned earlier that made it feel unconditional. Best drug I ever had.
I don’t know whether that unconditional love ended up being true. I think it was true in a part of her, and it may also have been the BPD idealization. You have to look at everything from multiple angles. But when you’re in love, you see everything from the love angle. That’s the reality shift I’m talking about. It’s great if the ground underneath is prepared for it. If the rose-colored glasses go on when you’re with the wrong person, they make it even harder to understand what’s real.
So I became the father in a relationship where I wanted an equal. Part of what happened may have been that she eventually grew up, and a daughter who grows up leaves home.

windows.label: Human
windows.text: That wasn’t the whole story.

windows.label: Human
windows.text:
The two years in-between contained enough insanity for several lifetimes.
Looking back, I’m grateful I loved her. For three months after we broke up, I trained myself to replace missing her with loving her, and now, any time I think of her, I feel so much joy and love, which I send her way.
That doesn’t mean I’d advise somebody to knowingly enter a dangerous relationship because it may be worth it. Going in, it helps to recognize your pattern, stop idealizing without becoming suspicious and closed, and have some idea what you’re getting into.

windows.label: Human
windows.text:
Modern life barely has an intermediate stage between being interested in somebody and getting sexually entangled. One old example is bundling, a mostly extinct practice now especially associated with the Amish, even though it existed much more widely. Courting couples could spend the night together in bed, usually clothed, with the idea that they could talk and be close without having sex, which sounds a lot like the missing middle I’m talking about.
Well, it didn’t exactly solve the problem: in late-1700s New England, where lots of couples bundled, 30–40 percent of brides were already pregnant on their wedding day. I’m not trying to bring bundling back. I just think we need some stage that everybody recognizes, where two people can explore tenderness and attraction without immediately sliding toward sex, moving in together, and a life bond.

windows.label: Human
windows.text:
And the question is more than just a practical one. It’s philosophical. Men have this (often subconscious) insecurity inside the provider role: how much does she love me, and how much does she love what I can do for her?
I don’t need the answer to be that what I provide has nothing to do with it. Maybe she likes that I’m competent, protective, useful, and can make things happen. I definitely like her beauty and her sexuality. I just want what we have to grow bigger than whatever first made us want each other. Because as Bee always said, “You’re either going up, or going down.”
I had wondered for years how much a woman would love me if I couldn’t really provide for her. Then Bee told me, “I would rather be with you in the forest than with any other man in a mansion.” That’s what made me fall in love with her.
I got a smaller and much less romantic test later. Bee gave me some shoes to try that didn’t fit. I wore them for a day, and somehow my knee ended up messed up for about a month. She did nurse me, but a bit reluctantly. She also kept suggesting it was partly in my head, or not really that bad. I get it, neither of us could believe one day in the wrong shoes could do that, but it still felt like she was brushing me off because she wanted my knee to be fine.
Before me, Bee had also stayed with a boyfriend who was totally broke and crazy and supported him for a while. Later she blamed herself for staying through that, and I agree. Helping carry somebody through a temporary incapacity, like my knee, is different from becoming the permanent support system for a man who won’t take responsibility. Some women are fixer types, which can create the opposite pattern.
What makes me desirable is not the same question as what makes me loved when I temporarily stop being desirable in that particular way.

windows.label: Human
windows.text:
Here’s the funny thing about labels: you can call someone your boyfriend or girlfriend for years and still have one foot out the door, but the word at least shows pretty fast whether you both think you’re in the same relationship.
True commitment grows out of relational depth, not a label: if we spend hours telling each other our deepest longings, fears, and problems, I’ll naturally be ready to help when you need me. I don’t need to promise that on paper. If someone says “I love you, I feel you, I’m here for you,” yet they hardly ever talk to you about what matters, that’s a red flag.
The person getting more of what they want may think the arrangement is fulfilling. Usually they’re just less aware that it isn’t. In college I had a friend with four girlfriends who boasted about it to girls while trying to get a fifth. I asked him, “But are you really happy?” He said, “No, I’m miserable, dude. I feel empty inside.”
The full conversation is so big that almost nobody would have casual sex if they took it seriously. Which is why almost nobody has the full conversation. I can’t decide what is okay for anybody else. I can say that most people who defend casual sex are not being very honest with themselves about pregnancy, attachment, or what they might owe the person afterward.
Outside a loving poly community or tribe, I think honest casual sex is almost impossible. If you want something closer to “casual love-making” without quite so many ways to damage each other, you probably need to find a free-love community where the people aren’t disposable, the bonds can be acknowledged, and any children have a village. But if the community is specifically designed to prioritize free love, you might find it attracts people who have traumas that produce trouble with connecting deeply, as ex-Tamera leader, Martin Winiecki wrote about after leaving recently.
This is a horrible catch-22. Wounded people get lonely, and loneliness itself can kill. But the wounds that make somebody desperate for a relationship may also make them a terrible person to be in one with. People don’t only trigger each other and learn lessons. Sometimes they terrorize or kill each other.
I’m pretty conservative about this. I would tell most of my friends not to date yet. First love your inner child. If you can’t even do that, forget a relationship for now. Get a cat or a puppy. If you’re dishonest, can’t care what happens to another person, or keep turning every relationship into the same disaster, come on.

windows.label: Human
windows.text: You’re not ready.

windows.label: Human
windows.text:
You don’t have to be completely healed, but the present-day adult has to be able to parent whatever intimacy wakes up inside you, and responsible enough to deal with an actual child if sex creates one. If you can’t be a parent in either sense, you aren’t ready to date.
A good relationship can teach you self-love too, which is part of the problem: you may need one most when you’re least capable of creating a good one, recognizing one, or keeping it good. It depends what each of you are ready for and have the resources for. Here’s a video that can help understand the long process.
